text.p: Blue-chip stocks rallied Wednesday after a week-long decline, and bonds rose after a strong turn-out at the Treasury's $7 billion sale of its first 10-year securites tied to inflation.
The dollar vaulted to its highest level against the Japanese yen in just under four years amid a growing sense that Japan will put up with weakness in its currency.

The Dow Jones industrial average ended up 84.66 points at 6,740.74, its best gain since Jan. 3, when it surged 102 points. But in the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,239 to 1,156 on heavy volume of 496 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Analysts said the market's extreme volatility prompted investors to seek the relative safety of big-name blue-chip stocks.
"Today the name of the game was the blue chips," said Peter Coolidge, senior equity trader at Brean Murray & Co. "There's still a lot of nervousness in the small cap names."
The cautious mood also was reflected in Nasdaq's performance, said analysts. The technology-laden Nasdaq Composite index managed only a fractional gain of 0.80 of a point to 1,355.17.

Analysts said several upcoming events were pivotal for the market's overall outlook, particularly Friday's fourth-quarter gross domestic product report and Thursday's testimony by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan on the state of the economy before the Senate Finance Committee. Greenspan's testimony begins at 10 a.m.

"Unless one of those events produces a surprise, the market should try to rally here," said Dan Ascani, president and director of research at Global Market Strategists Inc. "A bounce of some kind here would be normal."
Even if stocks do manage a near-term recovery, Ascani said, "We're about out of January now, so the market will probably have a rough road ahead."

The concern is that when January ends, with it may go the furious inflow of retirement fund cash that has provided an important source of market momentum, particularly for big-name stocks, which have boomed in recent months.
In the bond market, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond rose 7/32 of a point, or $2.19 per $1,000 face value, which lowered its yield to 6.91 percent from Tuesday's close of 6.93 percent.

The dollar rose to 122.13 yen in late trading from 121.00 late Tuesday. It touched a peak of 122.75 yen, its highest level since early February 1993, in Asian trade. The dollar fell to 1.6440 German marks from 1.6480 marks Tuesday.
Coffee prices continued to surge on worries that crop problems will cut supplies later this year.
At New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, March delivery coffee closed 5.10 cents higher at 144.60 cents a pound -- up 40 percent from its close on Dec. 6.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybeans led grain markets higher on talk the South American harvest would be delayed by rains. Such delays could prompt foreign buying of futures to lock in a delivery price for soybeans.
March soybeans ended 5-1/2 cents a bushel higher at $7.50.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 share index ended 29.9 points lower at 4,207.5. In Tokyo, the Nikkei average of 225 leading shares, jumped by 538.73 points or 3.03 percent, to close at 18,335.30.
